My AI policy

If a project doesn't have an AI_POLICY.md, this is my personal policy:

  • All AI assisted commits will have an Assisted-by: <Harness>:<model> trailer.
  • All AI generated text in descriptions, comments, etc. will be marked by 🤖 _AI text below_ 🤖 or otherwise clearly indicated (detail block, etc)
  • Mechanical changes that don't make a commit (like a rebase) might not have a marker since there's no place to put one.

I oversee all changes directly (I don't use unattended harnesses) and usually hand edit at least a little.

Hi there 👋, I'm Ben

  • 😄 Pronouns: he/him
  • 📫 How to reach me: email or BlueSky @fringetracker.bsky.social

I am an Associate Professor of Statistical Data Science at Macquarie University in Sydney, leading an Astrostatistics Research Group. Before this, I was a Senior Lecturer in Astrophysics and ARC DECRA Fellow at the University of Queensland, a NASA Sagan Fellow at NYU, and I did my DPhil at Balliol College, Oxford.

I research extrasolar planets - planets around other stars - and focus on developing and applying new data science approaches for detecting and characterizing them.

Currently, I'm working on exoplanet direct imaging with JWST's Aperture Masking Interferometer and coronagraphs, interferometry with VLTI, and preparation for the Lazuli Space Observatory. I'm also interested in using radio astronomy to study planets' magnetic interactions with their host stars, and modelling radiocarbon in tree rings as a tracer of ancient solar activity.

Slides for my talks are available here.

some repos

I've contributed to a number of open-source packages for physics, such as

  • virgil, a Jax package for interferometric data analysis
  • dLux, a Jax & equinox library for differentiable, GPU accelerated physical optics
    • docs here!
    • papers at arXiv:2011.09780 and arXiv:2107.00952
    • dLux is a full rewrite of morphine, a physical optics simulation library forked from poppy using Jax for autodiff
  • ticktack, a carbon box modelling library for analysing tree ring radiocarbon data
    • docs here
  • halophot, a pipeline for extracting precise photometry from even very saturated K2 and TESS data
    • papers at arXiv:1708.07462 and arXiv:1908.06981
  • keplersmear, a pipeline for Kepler and K2 using collateral 'smear' data to recover missing lightcurves of bright stars
    • papers at arXiv:1510.00008 and arXiv:1905.09831
  • k2sc, a pipeline for calibrating K2 photometry using Gaussian Processes
    • paper at arXiv:1603.09167
    • docs here

J. Emmanuel Johnson

Research scientist and scientific software engineer · differentiable Earth observation in JAX
UNEP IMEO · Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) · Valencia, Spain

GeoStack docs · Research notebook · LinkedIn · X / Twitter

I build the software that turns satellite and in-situ observations into numbers someone can act on, each with an honest error bar. The physics is differentiable, the inference is Bayesian, and every step is checked against a trusted oracle. All of it lives in one open-source JAX stack: GeoStack.

The stack

Earth observation code usually means gluing together a reader, a regridder, a physics model, an inverse method and an ML model that were never designed to meet. GeoStack is the opposite: small libraries with one contract each, laid out along the data-maturity axis from raw instrument output (L0) to decisions (L5). The science axis says what each level means. The compute between two levels is where physics and inference live. The engineering axis underneath says how the data is stored, carried and composed at every level.

How the packages layer: imports only point down, and CI proves the graph has no cycles

Layer Library What it does
GeoStack geotoolz Raster operators, STAC catalog and patching; geoarray, one geo-carrier for NumPy and JAX, with a differentiable affine transform
xrtoolz The same operator model on xarray: indices, temporal statistics, CF output
pipekit Composable Operator and pipeline protocols shared by every package
GeoNumerics gaussx Structured linear algebra: Kalman filters, GP primitives, block operators on lineax
finitevolX Finite-volume operators on staggered grids
spectraldiffx Spectral derivatives and solvers
GeoML vardax Variational data assimilation: 3D-Var, 4D-Var, optimal estimation
filterax Ensemble and Kalman filtering
pyrox · kernellib Gaussian processes and probabilistic NNs for NumPyro; kernels
geonnax Neural fields and basis functions for geoscience
gauss_flows Normalizing flows and SurVAE
optax_bayes The Bayesian learning rule as Optax optimizers
xtremax Extreme values with JAX and NumPyro
GeoModels radtrax Differentiable radiative transfer, matched filters, retrievals
plumax Plume physics: masks, integrated mass enhancement, flux, emission rates
somax Simple ocean models: quasi-geostrophic, shallow water

The method

Every problem in the stack follows the same ladder. Step 2, a slow but trusted physics-based inversion, is the oracle that every faster learned method must match before it ships.

Case studies

Methane: from radiance to emission rate

Detecting and quantifying methane plumes from EMIT, Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8/9. A layered Beer–Lambert forward model in radtrax gives the matched-filter target and every Jacobian by autodiff. The pipeline then runs matched filter, plume vetting and optimal estimation through vardax. plumax turns the column enhancement into an emission rate in kg/h.

The full methane walkthrough, from scene catalog to served model

Sea surface height: from altimetry tracks to gap-free maps

Mapping the ocean's mesoscale from sparse along-track altimetry. OceanBench: The Sea Surface Height Edition (NeurIPS 2023, Datasets and Benchmarks) is a benchmark and toolkit for SSH interpolation (docs, code). The methods range from optimal interpolation and neural fields (ml4ssh, knerf, functa4eo) to quasi-geostrophic models in somax inside 4D-Var.

How it came together

GeoStack is not a fresh start; it is ten years of research code, rebuilt so the pieces fit.

Older work still worth a look: rbig (Rotation-Based Iterative Gaussianization and information measures), jbayesevt (Bayesian extreme value models), manipy (semi-supervised manifold learning), keras-fairkl (fair kernel learning), and my research notebook of notes and tutorials.

How I work

  • JAX all the way down. Equinox modules, with jit, vmap and grad through the physics, and float64 where the maths needs it.
  • Tested against the truth. Every refactor merges behind numeric gates: parity with the code it replaces, autodiff against finite differences, closed-form oracles.
  • Small packages, explicit seams. Heavy dependencies sit behind optional extras, and everything is MIT-licensed.

Interests: atmospheric retrievals · data assimilation · Gaussian processes and uncertainty quantification · neural fields · extremes · ML for dynamical systems.

Built on

GeoStack stands on the shoulders of these open-source projects, and the packages above are designed to compose with them rather than replace them.

JAX numerics · JAX · Equinox · jaxtyping · lineax · diffrax · optimistix · matfree · finitediffx · interpax · einx · einops

Probabilistic ML and training · NumPyro · Optax · FlowJAX · BlackJAX · Grain · Orbax

Geospatial data · xarray · georeader (GeoTensor) · rasterio · rioxarray · GeoPandas · Shapely · pyproj · xvec · regionmask · xrft

Cloud-native storage and catalogs · obstore · async-geotiff · Zarr · fsspec · Dask · DuckDB · PyArrow · pystac · pystac-client

Data access · earthaccess · Planetary Computer · Earth Engine · Copernicus Marine · CDS API · HITRAN

The scientific Python base · NumPy · SciPy · scikit-learn · scikit-image · pandas

A special thanks to Patrick Kidger's JAX ecosystem: Equinox, lineax, diffrax, optimistix and jaxtyping are the backbone of nearly every package here.
